Slide 1

Classifying Kidney Transplant Rejection from Biopsy RNA

Approximate pacing: 0:20 on this slide · Talk 0:00–0:20

Delivery cues · not read aloud

Introduce the analysis and software, then define transplant rejection and biopsy measurements.

This project uses RNA measurements from kidney biopsies to classify rejection. I will show two parts of the work: a comparison of logistic regression and CatBoost, and the software I built to reproduce the analysis and make the selected model available through a scoring service and prototype application.

Sources and evidence
  • NIDDK: Kidney biopsy
  • NIDDK: Kidney transplant
  • Project research context
  • Banff Reference Guide, Banff-Kidney-2024-3, updated April 20, 2026: validated biopsy transcript diagnostics in antibody-mediated rejection assessment

Slide 2

Transplant rejection and kidney biopsy

Approximate pacing: 0:55 on this slide · Talk 0:20–1:15

Delivery cues · not read aloud

Read the definitions in order. Introduce the two types of measurement aloud, then move to the project purpose. Leave the clinical and research context to slide 4.

A kidney transplant gives a person a donor kidney. The recipient's immune system can recognize it as foreign and attack it. That immune response is rejection.

A kidney biopsy is a small tissue sample collected from the kidney for examination. There are two types of measurement. The first is histology, which is a microscopic examination that reveals injury and inflammation, which can support a rejection diagnosis.

The second is molecular measurements. These are counts of selected RNA types that reflect gene activity in the mix of cells in the tissue. RNA includes messages cells make when genes are active. More immune cells in a specimen can also change its RNA pattern.

This project uses those molecular measurements to compare classifiers and build a scoring application.

Sources and evidence
  • NIDDK: Kidney biopsy
  • NIDDK: Kidney transplant
  • Project research context
  • Zhang et al., 2024, Methods and Table 2: allograft diagnoses rescored using Banff 2019 criteria
  • September 19 full-study review with exact source pages
  • Banff Reference Guide, Banff-Kidney-2024-3, updated April 20, 2026: validated biopsy transcript diagnostics in antibody-mediated rejection assessment

Slide 3

Purpose of this project

Approximate pacing: 1:05 on this slide · Talk 1:15–2:20

Delivery cues · not read aloud

Connect the binary endpoint to treatment-related assessment and briefly explain both error consequences. Give the model comparison and software aims equal weight. Describe the score as a potential additional source of evidence, with the current evaluation against recorded diagnoses. Leave Banff, Zhang and the KDIGO recommendation to the next slide.

Whether rejection is present can affect decisions about further treatment to suppress the immune system. Missed rejection can leave kidney injury untreated, while unnecessary treatment can worsen an infection. A binary molecular score could provide additional evidence during that assessment, while subtype and other findings would still guide treatment.

The first part is model comparison. How do logistic regression and CatBoost compare in classifying any recorded rejection versus no rejection from B-HOT biopsy RNA, particularly in missed cases and incorrect flags? I evaluate them against the recorded diagnoses on the same specimens.

The second part is software engineering. I made preprocessing, training and evaluation reproducible, then built a tested scoring service and prototype application. They let a user submit compatible RNA counts and inspect the selected model score, its threshold and the rejection flag. An analyst can try the model through the application, and other software can call the service.

Sources and evidence
  • Zhang et al., 2024, Discussion, page 13: treatment-related rationale and infection controls
  • KDIGO transplant-recipient guideline summary, 2009, recommendations 6.1–6.4
  • Clinical motivation, potential use and the two project aims
  • The scoring service and public specimen demonstration
  • Second International Consensus Guidelines on BK Polyomavirus, 2024
  • Source review of biopsy findings, care decisions and error consequences

Slide 4

Clinical and research context

Approximate pacing: 1:10 on this slide · Talk 2:20–3:30

Delivery cues · not read aloud

Explain Banff and Zhang, then the Biopsy and treatment row. Expand KDIGO as Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes if needed. Retain the exception for substantial treatment delay. The two error consequences were introduced on slide 3.

Banff is a framework specialists use to classify transplant biopsy findings. Its current guidance includes thoroughly validated biopsy transcript tests in defined settings for antibody-mediated rejection. That gives molecular assessment an established clinical context. It does not confer that validation on my classifier.

Zhang and colleagues provide the public B-HOT data. Their four-class study already compared regularized regression with other approaches, including gradient boosting. They selected LASSO, a form of regularized regression, because accuracy was similar and it can use fewer weighted features. Their result is a reason to take the simpler comparator seriously.

Biopsy findings also help guide treatment. KDIGO recommends biopsy before treating acute rejection, unless waiting would substantially delay treatment. This connects the assessment of biopsy findings to a treatment decision. It does not establish that my model improves that decision.

Sources and evidence

  • Implemented methods compared with the source study
  • KDIGO transplant-recipient guideline summary, 2009, recommendation 6.1
  • Zhang et al., Supplementary Methods: algorithm comparison and LASSO selection

Slide 5

What the dataset contains

Approximate pacing: 1:10 on this slide · Talk 3:30–4:40

Delivery cues · not read aloud

Point to the shared specimen ID. Explain why native controls can help distinguish non-rejection inflammation, then qualify the evaluated population. Say separation is not documented, without claiming that patients or centers overlapped.

I assembled the public downloads into these two tables. The count table has one row per specimen and 770 RNA measurements. The specimen-information table supplies the recorded diagnosis and study group. Specimen ID joins the rows one to one, so GSM6510425 identifies the same specimen in both tables.

Of the 1,395 specimens, 1,193 are transplant biopsies and 202 are native-kidney controls, meaning the person's own kidneys. These controls include normal tissue, but also inflammation from infection or other disease. They help distinguish rejection from other causes of inflammation, rather than making every inflammatory signal a rejection signal.

That is useful, but it also changes the population being tested. Discovery contains 191 native controls and validation only 11. I included all specimens, and the public metadata do not identify the native controls individually, so I cannot report transplant-only performance.

The paper calls the validation cohort independent, but does not document separation by patient or referring center. The public metadata lack those identifiers, so I cannot verify separation. This does not establish that overlap occurred. All specimens were processed at Arkana Laboratories.

Slide 6

Outcome: rejection versus no rejection

Approximate pacing: 0:40 on this slide · Talk 4:40–5:20

Delivery cues · not read aloud

Show how the three rejection diagnoses share one label. Give the two excluded-category examples aloud. The number removed for these diagnoses is unreported; do not confuse it with the 40 specimens removed after assay quality checks.

Antibody-mediated rejection involves immune proteins called antibodies. T-cell-mediated rejection involves immune cells called T cells. Mixed rejection includes both. I combine those three diagnoses as rejection, against the recorded no-rejection category.

The authors excluded borderline acute T-cell-mediated rejection, where findings are suspicious but fall short of the full criteria, and chronic inactive antibody-mediated rejection. The paper does not report how many cases these diagnostic exclusions removed, so I cannot give a percentage. They matter because the comparison leaves out categories where interpreting the findings can be difficult.

I retained the original diagnoses as well, so I could check where the missed cases occurred.

Slide 7

The measurements used to build the features

Approximate pacing: 0:45 on this slide · Talk 5:20–6:05

Delivery cues · not read aloud

Use the 758 and 12 groups to explain the role of each set of counts.

Each specimen has 770 counts of selected RNA types. The 758 model measurements include human and viral RNA. Their signals reflect both gene activity and the mixture of cells in the biopsy. Their normalized values become the model's inputs.

The other 12 measure relatively stable housekeeping RNAs. More usable RNA entering the assay can raise counts across many measurements. The reference helps adjust for that overall difference.

I used the housekeeping counts for normalization, then excluded them from the model. The next slide shows the calculation.

Slide 8

Preparing counts for the model

Approximate pacing: 1:00 on this slide · Talk 6:05–7:05

Delivery cues · not read aloud

Walk down the four numbered steps, using IFNG for the arithmetic.

For each of the 758 counts, I used the same four steps. The right side follows IFNG in my public example, starting with its raw count of four.

Add one and take the base-two logarithm. Adding one allows zero counts, and the logarithm compresses the range. For IFNG, log base two of five is about 2.322.

Next, do that same transformation for each of the 12 housekeeping counts and average them. In this specimen, the reference is about 7.900.

Subtract that reference from each transformed count. For IFNG, 2.322 minus 7.900 gives minus 5.578. So the final value describes the target's signal relative to the reference level. The same raw count can produce a different normalized value in a specimen with a different reference. Those 758 normalized values are the model inputs.

Slide 9

Development and evaluation specimens

Approximate pacing: 0:45 on this slide · Talk 7:05–7:50

Delivery cues · not read aloud

Follow discovery into training and screening, briefly clarify the terminology, then move to the separate validation box. Keep the authors’ cohort names on the slide.

The authors supplied 1,050 discovery specimens and 345 validation specimens. I preserved that division.

Within discovery, I split 787 specimens into training and 263 into screening, keeping diagnosis proportions similar. Training fitted the models. Screening selected the model and threshold.

The screening split serves the role often called a validation set. The authors' validation cohort is my final test set.

Once the choices were fixed, I evaluated the models on those same 345 specimens. That checks how the selected model and threshold perform on other specimens.

Slide 10

Models compared

Approximate pacing: 1:00 on this slide · Talk 7:50–8:50

Delivery cues · not read aloud

Explain each model in table order.

Each model produces a rejection score. I call it a score because calibration has not established reliable individual probabilities here.

The constant model uses the training rejection fraction for everyone. It shows what happens without RNA measurements.

IFNG encodes interferon gamma, an immune-signalling protein associated with T-cell-mediated rejection. I used logistic regression with this one normalized measurement as a simple benchmark. It was fixed in the starting recipe, rather than selected as the best individual predictor.

The all-RNA model also used logistic regression, but combined all 758 normalized measurements using learned weights. Regularization limited those weights to reduce overfitting.

CatBoost can capture nonlinear patterns and interactions. One RNA measurement's relationship with rejection can depend on another measurement's level. It works with numerical inputs, so categorical features are not required. Shallow trees and a small learning rate help limit overfitting.

The comparison uses the same specimens and normalization. The main comparison is all-RNA logistic regression versus CatBoost, with IFNG and the constant model as supporting benchmarks. I examine how their missed rejection and false positives differ.

Slide 11

Selecting the model and threshold

Approximate pacing: 0:55 on this slide · Talk 8:50–9:45

Delivery cues · not read aloud

Explain each denominator, then the screening rule and the five-versus-six result. Keep the original selection distinct from the later validation comparison.

A threshold turns a score into a rejection flag. Recall starts with all cases diagnosed as rejection and counts how many the model flags correctly. Precision starts with all rejection flags and counts how many agree with a recorded rejection diagnosis.

I chose a screening target of at least 90 percent recall, then minimized false positives. ROC-AUC broke ties. This was an experiment choice, not a clinical requirement.

Both models detected 157 of 174 screening rejection cases. CatBoost made five false positives among 89 no-rejection specimens. Logistic regression made six. That one-case difference selected CatBoost under the rule.

I kept the selected model and threshold fixed for evaluation. Screening explains the original selection. The separate validation results show how the models compared afterward. Choosing a threshold does not calibrate the score.

Sources and evidence
  • Saved discovery screening counts
  • Training, threshold and selection procedure
  • Review of the model-selection evidence

Slide 12

Validation results

Approximate pacing: 1:40 on this slide · Talk 9:45–11:25

Delivery cues · not read aloud

Use the chart's missed-cases and incorrect-flags labels. Explain the CatBoost/logistic difference and uncertainty. Identify the colored sentence as follow-up screening selections. Describe the revised discovery procedure and distinguish its supporting assessment from author validation. End with the IFNG tradeoff, then the constant baseline.

These results use the same 345 validation specimens: missed cases among 169 recorded as rejection, and incorrect flags among 176 recorded as no rejection.

IFNG missed 14 cases and incorrectly flagged 75. All-RNA logistic regression missed 33 and incorrectly flagged eight. CatBoost missed 25 and also incorrectly flagged eight.

CatBoost therefore missed eight fewer cases than logistic regression, with the same number of incorrect flags. That adds evidence in its favor beyond the narrow screening result. The paired 95 percent bootstrap interval for the recall difference includes zero, though, so a dependable advantage remains uncertain.

CatBoost’s narrow screening advantage prompted a follow-up with 20 random discovery splits, keeping diagnosis proportions similar. Each used 630 specimens for training, 210 for screening and 210 for assessment. This procedure used fewer training specimens and revised candidate settings, held fixed across repetitions. Screening chose settings, thresholds and the preferred family. Assessment checked both family winners afterward. The original 345 validation specimens were unused.

Screening selected CatBoost 13 times and logistic regression seven. The preferred model changed with the discovery split, so logistic regression remains a credible simpler alternative. The repetitions reuse specimens.

Compared with IFNG, CatBoost makes 67 fewer incorrect flags but misses 11 more cases. Its validation recall is 85.2 percent, below the 90 percent screening target. The preferred tradeoff depends on how the result would be used.

The constant model flags everyone at its threshold of 0.5. It misses no rejection cases but incorrectly flags all 176 no-rejection specimens.

Sources and evidence
  • Same-specimen error comparison
  • Editable presentation evidence
  • Discovery-only stability follow-up, 20 overlapping repetitions
  • Full-study review and September 22 source recheck

Browser stop 2 of 3

A public specimen in the application

Approximate pacing: 2:15 in the browser · Talk 12:55–15:10

Delivery cues · not read aloud

The Application tab contains the CSV preview and one Kidney biopsy application link. That link opens a separate tab. The No Rejection example and Get research score control produce the public specimen result.

Try an incomplete file clears the prior result and displays Missing required assay targets: IFNG.

If the service is unavailable, the separate demo_fallback.html contains captured application screenshots. The fallback wording is: “These are captured responses from the same application.” They are not live requests.

The engineering-page tab remains open. Its Engineering tab continues with the shared calculation.

This preview shows selected columns from the actual input CSV. Each row represents a specimen, with its identifier followed by seven hundred and seventy raw counts. The full input includes all twelve housekeeping targets. The application link opens the working service in a separate tab. An analyst or molecular laboratory researcher can use it without running the training scripts.

I will use this public specimen, GSM6510425. It comes from the discovery-screen group and has a recorded no-rejection diagnosis. The prepared examples were selected by accession within each diagnosis, rather than by whether the model got them right. This is a software demonstration, separate from the validation result.

The request supplies all seven hundred and seventy raw counts. The diagnosis is displayed for comparison, but it is not sent as a predictor. The application calls the service and shows the preparation for IFNG as one example. Four counts become about two point three two two after the log transformation. Subtracting the housekeeping reference gives about minus five point five seven eight. The same operation prepares the full model input.

The model score is about zero point two seven five, below the frozen threshold of about zero point eight seven seven. The rejection flag is false. The score and threshold are separate, and the model version tells us which saved calculation produced them.

Now I will remove IFNG. The application clears the previous result, identifies the missing measurement, and returns no new score. It does not silently fill the missing value. The user gets an explanation they can act on.

Browser stop 3 of 3

The shared calculation and software checks

Approximate pacing: 4:00 in the browser · Talk 15:10–19:10

Delivery cues · not read aloud

Shared calculation, about 1:10: the preparation sequence leads to the training and prediction source excerpts. Both call normalize_counts. The code guide supplies further detail.

Programmatic access, about 1:10: the request precedes the response-field explanation. Complete saved JSON response expands the actual HTTP 200 response. The missing-IFNG example follows it.

Verification and setup, about 1:40: the cohort and comparison are explained before the agreement table. Recorded agreement check opens the historical record. Failure cases and setup evidence follow, with dates and local versus hosted scope identified.

Closing slide 14 provides the transition back to PowerPoint.

The key implementation decision was to share the preparation and prediction code. Otherwise, the application could produce a different result from the analysis even while loading the same fitted model.

On the left, the training procedure reads the RNA counts and calls normalize_counts. On the right, the application entry point calls that same function before it scores the specimen. The twelve housekeeping targets supply the within-specimen reference. The remaining seven hundred and fifty-eight targets become model inputs. Any learned scaling or feature selection is fitted on training data and saved with the model.

The application and command-line interface both use Predictor.predict. That makes the calculation reusable without duplicating it in the browser. The browser handles choosing input and displaying the response. The service handles validation and scoring. The complete code guide is available here, but these are the source excerpts that explain the main decision.

The next view shows how other software can call it. An API is a documented interface for exchanging data. Here the caller sends a CSV to POST /predict. This is the exact public input used in the example, available to download. A laboratory research tool or a batch script could send the same request.

The response identifies the specimen and returns the model score, threshold, rejection flag, model version and expected schema version. Those fields let a caller interpret and record the result. The missing-IFNG response uses HTTP status four twenty-two with a concise explanation and no predictions. The same input rules apply whether the request comes from the page or another program.

The final view shows how I checked agreement. I sent all three hundred and forty-five validation specimens through the HTTP service and compared the responses with command-line predictions and the saved research results. The flags matched, and the score differences were below the tolerance shown here. The check included reordered measurement columns, because valid files should be matched by target name rather than accidental column position.

This is a software consistency check. It does not create another estimate of classifier performance. The saved record identifies the model and source files checked. Other tests cover failures such as duplicate measurements and incompatible model metadata.

For handoff, another developer receives the locked environment, commands to reproduce the analysis and start the service, automated checks, and a tested local container with the research model. The hosted workflow passed for an earlier revision; the application and research-container evidence shown here was recorded locally. A cloud deployment remains future work.

Together, the reports make the analysis inspectable, the application makes the model usable, and the shared code and checks keep the software connected to the evaluated procedure. I will return to the slideshow to close.

Slide 14

What this project accomplished

Approximate pacing: 0:50 on this slide · Talk 19:10–20:00

Delivery cues · not read aloud

Return to PowerPoint on slide 14. Summarize the completed model comparison and software engineering, acknowledge the public data and AI assistance, then invite questions.

To return to the two project aims: in the model comparison, CatBoost missed eight fewer validation rejection cases than logistic regression, with eight incorrect flags each. The uncertainty and repeated discovery splits leave a dependable advantage unsettled.

For software engineering, I made the analysis reproducible and built a tested scoring service and prototype application. Another user can inspect the evidence, submit compatible counts and identify the model and threshold behind the result.

Zhang and colleagues supplied the public data. AI assisted with development and this presentation. Thank you.
